units.d: Life first: prayer is a relationship with the Father before it is a skill.
The Bible is my standard and the Spirit is my guide: learning to pray by God’s heart.

units.t: The Ministry of Praying for Others
units.d: Then ministry: from praying for ourselves to standing in the gap for others.
Build God’s system: praying in one accord and passing prayer on.

lessons.title: Prayer Is a Relationship with the Father
lessons.sub: Enter your inner room, shut the door, and build your relationship with God first
lessons.hear:
When many people hear the words “prayer ministry,” they picture the laying on of hands at the front of a church, loud cries at a prayer meeting, or intercession beside a hospital bed. These are all precious ministries. Yet the first thing Jesus taught about prayer was not set in a public place but in a small room with the door shut: “But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.” (Matthew 6:6)

Jesus first points out a dangerous kind of prayer. The hypocrites “love to stand and pray in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men.” On the surface this prayer speaks to God, but in reality it performs for people; its focus is not on God but on self. This is the self-centered life of the old self: even prayer becomes a way to build our own image. Jesus says, “they have received their reward.” People saw, the applause came, and the reward ends there.

The inner room is a picture. In ancient Israelite homes, the inner room was often a small, windowless storeroom for grain. There was no audience and no applause, only you and the Father. The foundation of prayer is this kind of hidden relationship. Think of a tree: people see the branches, leaves and fruit, but not the roots driven deep into the ground. Public prayer ministry is the branches; secret prayer is the root. The deeper the roots go, the higher the branches can grow.

Jesus also says, “In praying, don’t use vain repetitions as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking.” The power of prayer is not in word count or volume but in relationship. A child does not need to memorize a speech before talking to his father; “your Father knows what things you need before you ask him.” (Matthew 6:8) We do not pray to persuade an unwilling God; we return to a Father who already knows and already loves us.

So the first lesson of 321 prayer ministry is not how to pray for others, but how to be the Father’s child. Life first, then relationships, then ministry; and in relationships, our relationship with God comes first, then with ourselves, with others and with our work. A person without an inner room may pray fluently in front of others, yet only be draining himself. A person who often meets the Father in the inner room carries heaven’s presence even when he says just one sentence.
lessons.light: When the self-centered pray, they wonder, “Do people think I pray well?” When the selfless pray, they think, “The Father is here, and I am with him.” Our focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. When the door of the inner room closes, the performance ends and the relationship begins. The first step of prayer ministry is not learning more words but letting Jesus reign in my prayers.
think: In Matthew 6:5-8, what two wrong ways of praying does Jesus mention? What problem do they share?
Where is my “inner room” right now? Is there a time in my day that belongs only to me and the Father?
If prayer is a relationship rather than a performance, what concrete changes would that bring to my prayers?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you that you are the Father who sees in secret. I confess that I often turn prayer into a performance for others, and often use many words to try to persuade you. Forgive my self-centered heart. Today I choose to enter the inner room, shut the door, and come to you alone. Holy Spirit, help me to be still and to know you as my Father, who already knows what I need. May my prayer first be a relationship with you, and then a channel for serving others. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.
prac: Choose your inner room
Pick a fixed place and time, such as ten minutes after you wake up, as your daily inner room with the Father.
Shut three doors
Shut off phone notifications, shut out the noise around you, and shut out the thought of “what others think of me.”
Address him before you ask
Spend a minute or two simply calling him “Father” and thanking him for who he is, without rushing to make requests.
Speak honestly
In your ordinary voice, tell the Father what you truly feel today, without polishing it.
Listen in silence
Leave two quiet minutes at the end, and write down a verse or a prompting the Holy Spirit brings to mind.
lessons.do: Today, choose your “inner room”: one place and one time. Spend ten minutes there doing just one thing: call God your Father, speak honestly to him, then be still for two minutes. Write one prompting from the Holy Spirit in your prayer journal.
deep: Is public prayer wrong, then?

Jesus did not forbid public prayer; he himself prayed in front of the crowd (John 11:41-42). The issue is not the setting but the motive: am I praying so people will see me, or so they will see the Father? When our prayer life in the inner room is solid, our public prayers will not slide into performance.
If God already knows what I need, why pray?

Prayer is not giving God the news; it is entering into relationship with the Father. Parents know when their child is hungry, yet they still love to hear the child ask. Prayer also changes us: when we bring our needs to God, our hearts turn from ourselves to him, from worry to trust.
lessons.quick: The foundation of prayer ministry is not the platform but the inner room; first be the Father’s child, then you can intercede for others.
text: “When you pray, you shall not be as the hypocrites, for they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men. Most certainly, I tell you, they have received their reward.
But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.
In praying, don’t use vain repetitions as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking.
Therefore don’t be like them, for your Father knows what things you need before you ask him.
lessons.keyText: But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.

lessons.title: Selfless Prayer
lessons.sub: Not my will, but yours, be done
lessons.hear:
In the Garden of Gethsemane we see the most honest and most anguished prayer in history. Jesus knew the cross was just ahead. “Being in agony he prayed more earnestly. His sweat became like great drops of blood falling down on the ground.” (Luke 22:44) This was not an easy prayer; it was the surrender of his whole life.

Jesus said, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42) This sentence has two parts. The first is honesty: Jesus did not pretend it did not hurt; he told the Father plainly what was in his heart. The second is surrender: he handed the final decision back to the Father. True prayer neither suppresses our feelings nor uses prayer to command God. It speaks honestly, then humbly lets go.

This is selfless prayer. The root of humanity’s fall is the self-centered life: wanting to be lord and king, wanting to take God’s place. Often our prayers are self-centered. We have already decided the answer and just want God to stamp it. If God does what we want, we say our prayer was answered; if not, we say God did not listen. Selfless prayer lets God be God and lets us be human: I may tell him my hopes, but I acknowledge that he is King.

This kind of prayer brings power. After Jesus prayed, “An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him.” (Luke 22:43) The cup was not removed, but strength came. Many times God does not change our circumstances, but he changes the life with which we face them. The disciples, by contrast, were found “sleeping because of grief.” Twice Jesus urged them to pray that they would not enter into temptation: “Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.” (Luke 22:46) Someone who does not pray can only rely on himself when temptation comes; someone who surrenders himself in prayer stands firm in the midst of it.

Those who serve by praying for others need to learn the prayer of Gethsemane first. When we pray for others, it is easy to bring in our own ideas, our own judgments, even our own desire to be seen. Only when we have said “not my will” in our own lives can we truly seek God’s will as we pray for others, rather than promoting our own.
lessons.light: The self-centered prayer of the old self says, “Let my will be done; God, please help.” The selfless prayer of the new self says, “Let your will be done; I am willing to follow.” Selflessness does not mean having no feelings; it means handing the final decision back to God. Only selflessness lets Jesus reign, only selflessness lets the Holy Spirit lead, and only selfless prayer carries strength from heaven.
think: In Jesus’ prayer in Luke 22:42, which part is honesty and which part is surrender?
Among my recent prayers, is there something I have already decided the answer to and just want God to approve?
If God does not take my “cup” away, can I still say, “Let your will be done”?
lessons.speak: Father, I tell you what is truly in my heart: there are things I fear and things I deeply want. If you are willing, please fulfill my hopes; nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done. Forgive me for so often trying to direct you through my prayers. As you strengthened Jesus, strengthen me too, so that I do not fall asleep in temptation but stand firm in prayer. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.
prac: Write down my cup
Write down one thing you have struggled with most lately and most want God to change.
Say it honestly
Tell the Father your feelings and hopes without polishing them, saying like Jesus, “if you are willing.”
Hand over the decision
Slowly and sincerely say, “Not my will, but yours, be done.”
Ask for strength, not just outcomes
Add one more line: “Whatever the outcome, please give me strength.”
Examine yourself before praying for others
Before praying for someone, ask yourself: am I seeking God’s will, or promoting my own?
lessons.do: Today, pray about one struggle the Gethsemane way: first say honestly how you feel, then hand the decision to the Father. Add it to your Prayer List, mark it “Entrusted,” and watch how God strengthens you.
deep: Does selfless prayer mean I can’t ask God for things?

No. Jesus himself made a request: “remove this cup from me.” God delights to hear our needs (Philippians 4:6). Selflessness is not being afraid to ask; it is leaving the outcome in God’s hands after we ask.
How can I tell whether I’m surrendering or just giving up?

Giving up says, “Forget it, God won’t listen anyway,” and the heart moves away from God. Selfless surrender says, “I trust that you know better than I what is good,” and the heart draws closer to God. The first brings discouragement; the second brings strength from heaven.
lessons.quick: Selfless prayer honestly says what I want, then lets God’s will be done.
text: He came out and went, as his custom was, to the Mount of Olives. His disciples also followed him.
When he was at the place, he said to them, “Pray that you don’t enter into temptation.”
He was withdrawn from them about a stone’s throw, and he knelt down and prayed,
saying, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”
An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him.
Being in agony, he prayed more earnestly. His sweat became like great drops of blood falling down on the ground.
When he rose up from his prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping because of grief,
and said to them, “Why do you sleep? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.”
lessons.keyText: saying, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”

lessons.title: Humble Prayer
lessons.sub: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble
lessons.hear:
Jesus told a parable: “Two men went up into the temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector.” From the outside, the Pharisee was a model believer: he fasted twice a week and gave tithes of all he received. His prayer was orderly, too, opening with thanks to God. But listen closely to what he thanked God for: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men: extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.”

This is a prayer centered on “I.” In name he spoke to God; in reality he compared and boasted before God. He “stood and prayed by himself,” which can also be understood as praying to himself. This is pride: leaving our proper place, grasping for power, wanting to take God’s place. He made himself not only his own judge but also the judge of others, placing the tax collector beneath himself.

But “the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’” (Luke 18:13) No long speech, no comparison, no excuses. He returned to his proper place as a human being: I am a sinner who needs grace. Jesus concluded, “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 18:14)

Humility is the key to revival. James says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) A proud prayer, however eloquent, is spoken to oneself; a humble prayer, even a single sentence, reaches straight to heaven. Humility means laying down power and returning to our proper place: letting people be people and letting God be God.

This is especially important for those in prayer ministry. When we often pray for others and see God answer, we can quietly begin to think it is because we are spiritual or gifted. Then we start to look down on those who struggle to pray, and to comment on other people’s problems in our prayers. At that point we have turned from the tax collector into the Pharisee. A true prayer minister always remembers that he too is a sinner who has received grace. We do not stand above people to pray for them; we stand with them before the throne of grace.
lessons.light: Pride provokes pride, and when pride meets pride, both lose. Humility inspires humility, and when humility meets humility, both win. Comparing ourselves with others in prayer is pride; admitting in prayer that we need grace is humility. Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. The greatest protection for anyone in prayer ministry is to return often to the place of the tax collector.
think: How do the prayers of the Pharisee and the tax collector differ in posture, content and focus?
When I pray for others, do I secretly compare myself with them, judge them, or look down on them?
What does “laying down power and returning to our proper place” look like concretely in my prayer life?
lessons.speak: God, be merciful to me, a sinner. I confess that I often compare myself with others in prayer, and often treat the grace you give me as my own achievement. Forgive my proud heart, and help me lay down power and return to my proper place. Give me the heart of the tax collector, so that when I pray for others I do not stand above them but stand with them in your grace. You resist the proud and give grace to the humble; I choose humility. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.
prac: Check the pronouns
Recall a recent prayer of yours: did “I” appear more often, or “you”?
Confess before you intercede
Before praying for someone, admit in one sentence that you also need grace.
Don’t preach in prayer
When praying for someone, don’t use the prayer to point out their faults; simply place them in God’s hands.
Give God the credit
When you see a prayer answered, let your first words be, “This is God’s grace.”
Stand alongside
Instead of “I’ll pray for you,” say, “Let’s come before God together.”
lessons.do: Today, pray for someone you have looked down on or compared yourself with in your heart. First confess your pride, then sincerely bless them. Do not mention their faults in your prayer; simply ask God to pour out his grace on them.
deep: Does humility mean constantly saying I’m no good?

Humility is not putting yourself down but seeing yourself truly: I am loved, and I need grace. The tax collector did not say he was worthless; he simply came honestly before God asking for mercy. Humility is returning to our proper place, not losing our worth.
How can those in prayer ministry guard against spiritual pride?

Regularly let others pray for you and counsel you; when you see a miracle, give the glory to Jesus; confess your sins to one another and pray for one another with trusted spiritual companions (James 5:16). People who are truly known in relationships are less likely to lose themselves in their gifts.
lessons.quick: One humble “God, be merciful to me” outweighs a thousand proud words.
text: He also spoke this parable to certain people who were convinced of their own righteousness, and who despised all others:
“Two men went up into the temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed by himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men: extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.’
But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”
lessons.keyText: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

lessons.title: The Lord’s Prayer: Praying to Build God’s System
lessons.sub: Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth
lessons.hear:
When the disciples saw Jesus’ life of prayer, they asked him to teach them to pray. Jesus gave them a short yet all-encompassing prayer, the Lord’s Prayer. It is not only a passage to memorize; it is a map for prayer, showing us its order and its focus.

The Lord’s Prayer begins, “Our Father in heaven.” Not “my Father” but “our Father”: from the very first word, prayer places us in God’s family. Then come three requests, all about God: “may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:9-10) God first, then us; this is prayer in its proper place. Our focus is first on God’s name, God’s kingdom and God’s will, and only then on our needs.

Only in the second half does the prayer turn to us: daily bread, forgiveness of sins, deliverance from temptation and from the evil one. God cares about every need, from the food on our table, to forgiveness in our hearts, to spiritual battle. But these needs are brought under God’s kingdom. Think of a family: a child can of course ask his father for bread, but a mature child also cares about his father’s wishes and wants to join in the family’s great work.

The Lord’s Prayer closes, “For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.” (Matthew 6:13) This is the heart of 321: let Jesus reign, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The purpose of our prayer is to build God’s system, so that people keep the Lord’s name holy, God’s kingdom comes, and God’s will is done on earth as it is in heaven.

So the Lord’s Prayer is also a blueprint for prayer ministry. When we pray for a person, a family, a church or a city, we can follow its order: pray that God’s name be honored there, that God’s kingdom reign there, and that God’s will be done there; then pray for specific needs, forgiveness and protection; and finally give all the glory to God. Prayer like this is no longer just about solving problems; it establishes God’s rule on earth.
lessons.light: Self-centered prayer begins with “I want.” Prayer that belongs to God begins with “your name, your kingdom, your will.” The Lord’s Prayer sets the order of prayer right: God before us, the kingdom before our needs. When we pray the Lord’s Prayer, we let Jesus reign in our prayers, build God’s system on earth, and give the kingdom, the power and the glory entirely to God.
think: How does the focus of the first three requests in the Lord’s Prayer differ from the last three? Why does this order matter?
In my usual prayers, how much time do I give to God’s name, God’s kingdom and God’s will?
If I used the Lord’s Prayer to pray for my family or my church, how could I make each line specific?
lessons.speak: Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy, beginning in my home and on my lips. Let your Kingdom come in my family, my work and my church; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us today our daily bread. Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.
prac: Hallowed be your name
Begin with a sentence or two worshiping who God is, and ask that his name be honored in this person or place.
Your kingdom come
Ask God to rule and reign in this situation, and for Jesus to be King in it.
Your will be done
Ask for God’s will to be done, rather than first stating the answer you think is right.
Bread, forgiveness, protection
Pray for specific needs, for forgiveness in relationships, and for spiritual protection.
Glory to God
Close with “yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory,” giving the credit to God first.
lessons.do: Today, pray once for your family through the six petitions of the Lord’s Prayer. You can open the Lord’s Prayer mode in the Prayer Workshop and write out a specific request for each line, step by step.
deep: What is the difference between reciting the Lord’s Prayer and praying through it?

Reciting means saying the whole prayer through once; praying through it means expanding each line into your own words. Both are good: reciting helps us remember the order, and expanding helps us live that order in everyday life.
The Lord’s Prayer says “as we also forgive our debtors.” Do I have to forgive others to be forgiven?

The Lord’s Prayer reminds us that those who receive forgiveness must also live out forgiveness (Matthew 6:14-15). Forgiving others is not the price we pay for forgiveness, but the fruit that flows naturally from a forgiven life. An unforgiving heart will hinder us from experiencing God’s grace.
lessons.quick: The Lord’s Prayer teaches us to seek God’s name, God’s kingdom and God’s will first, and then our needs.
text: Pray like this: “‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread.
Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.’
lessons.keyText: Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

lessons.title: Praying God’s Word
lessons.sub: My words remain in you; ask whatever you desire
lessons.hear:
Many people say, “I don’t know how to pray. I don’t know what to say.” Jesus gave a very practical answer: “If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire, and it will be done for you.” (John 15:7) Where do the words of prayer come from? From the word of God.

Jesus used the picture of the vine and the branches. A branch does not bear fruit by straining on its own; it remains on the vine, the sap flows into it, and fruit grows naturally. “Apart from me you can do nothing.” Prayer is the same. When God’s words remain in us, God’s heart flows into ours; what we desire gradually lines up with what God desires, and such requests are answered.

Praying God’s word means turning Scripture into prayer. When we read, “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing,” we can say, “Lord, you are my shepherd; in what I lack today, please lead me.” When we read, “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God,” we do just that, handing our worries to God one by one. Scripture gives us direction and faith, because we are praying God’s own promises.

This is especially precious in prayer ministry. When we pray for others, human words are limited and may even carry our biases, but God’s word is living and active. For someone who is anxious, we can pray Philippians 4; for someone who is weak, Isaiah 40; for someone who has just lost a loved one, Psalm 23. We are not using Scripture as a magic formula; through God’s word we stand together with them on God’s promises.

The Bible is my standard. Someone who regularly reads God’s word prays with deep roots and firm foundations; someone who prays only by feeling will rise and fall with their emotions. Jesus said, “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples.” (John 15:8) Praying God’s word lets our prayers bear fruit and brings glory to the Father.
lessons.light: When we pray in our own strength, we run out of words; when we pray God’s word, the spring never runs dry. Change your thinking and you change your life. When God’s words remain in me, my perspective shifts from a human view to God’s view, from a temporary view to an eternal one, and my prayer shifts from “I want” to “God has promised.”
think: In John 15:7, what is the condition for answered prayer? How does it relate to the picture of the vine?
What passage of Scripture do I read most often? How could I turn it into a prayer?
When praying for a friend who is anxious, which passage could I use?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the vine and I am a branch. I confess that apart from you I can do nothing, not even pray. Let your words remain in me, and let your heart flow into mine. Today I pray according to your word: in nothing will I be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, I will make my requests known to you. May I bear much fruit, so that the Father is glorified. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.
prac: Choose a passage
Pick two or three verses from today’s reading, or use a passage from the Pray the Scriptures tool.
Read slowly three times
First for meaning, second to find the verbs and promises, third to find the line that moves you.
Change “he” to “you”
Turn the words that describe God into words spoken directly to God.
Add a name
When praying for someone, put that person’s name into the promise.
Stand on the promise
Close by saying, “Lord, I stand on this word of yours.”
lessons.do: Today, open Pray the Scriptures, choose a passage, and turn it into prayer using the five steps. Then use the same passage to pray once for a friend, and send the passage to them.
deep: Will praying Scripture lead me to take verses out of context?

First understand the context of the passage, then apply its principles. For example, from Old Testament promises given to Israel we can see God’s character and faithfulness, rather than applying them mechanically. The more fully we read, the more accurately we pray.
If I’m not familiar with the Bible, how do I start?

Start with the Psalms, which are prayers in themselves. Read one psalm a day and turn the line that moves you into your own prayer. You can also ask Xiaozhi to help you find suitable passages, then meditate on them slowly yourself.
lessons.quick: When God’s words remain in me, my prayers follow God’s heart.
text: I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
If a man doesn’t remain in me, he is thrown out as a branch and is withered; and they gather them, throw them into the fire, and they are burned.
If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire, and it will be done for you.
“In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples.
lessons.keyText: If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire, and it will be done for you.

lessons.title: Praying in the Spirit
lessons.sub: We don’t know how to pray as we ought, but the Spirit himself makes intercession for us
lessons.hear:
Sometimes prayer flows easily; at other times we cannot get a single word out. Facing a loved one’s serious illness, a broken marriage or a situation with no way out, we truly do not know what to ask for. Healing, or peace? A change of circumstances, or endurance? Paul says, “In the same way, the Spirit also helps our weaknesses, for we don’t know how to pray as we ought. But the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can’t be uttered.” (Romans 8:26)

This is a great comfort. Prayer is not an exam to see whether we can give the right answer. When we are weak and do not know how to pray, the Holy Spirit has not left us; he himself prays within us. “He who searches the hearts knows what is on the Spirit’s mind, because he makes intercession for the saints according to God.” (Romans 8:27) The Holy Spirit lives in our hearts, not in our heads. With groanings too deep for words, he carries the deepest needs of our hearts to the Father according to God’s will.

So the first lesson of praying in the Spirit is this: rely on the Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head. When we pray with our heads, we analyze, calculate and worry, and the more we think, the more troubled we become. When we pray with our hearts, we open ourselves to God and let the Holy Spirit lead, and our hearts gradually settle. This does not mean we stop thinking; it means our thinking submits to the Spirit’s leading. Use your heart and you find joy; use your head and you find worry.

The second lesson is listening. Praying in the Spirit is not only about speaking but also about listening. We can be still and ask the Holy Spirit: what should I pray for this person? A verse, a picture or an inner prompting may all be the Spirit’s leading. But these promptings must be tested by Scripture and shared with humility, because “we know in part” (1 Corinthians 13:9).

The third lesson is trust. Paul goes on, “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.” (Romans 8:28) Those who pray in the Spirit may not see the answer right away, but in prayer they receive the peace of entrusting everything to God. What those who pray for others need most is not more technique, but a heart led by the Holy Spirit.
lessons.light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. The self-centered prayer of the old self relies on our own minds, and the more we pray, the more anxious we become. The selfless prayer of the new self relies on the Spirit’s leading, and the more we pray, the more peace we have. The issues of life flow from the heart, and the Holy Spirit dwells in the heart, not in the head. Praying in the Spirit means yielding control and letting the Spirit pray within us and for us.
think: According to Romans 8:26-27, how does the Holy Spirit help us pray? What comfort does this give me?
When I pray, do I tend to use my “head” or my “heart”? How does that show?
Have I ever experienced a reminder or prompting from the Holy Spirit in prayer? How did I test it with Scripture?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, I confess there are many things I don’t know how to pray for. Thank you for helping me in my weakness and interceding for me with groanings which can’t be uttered. Help me stop relying on myself with my head, and instead rely on you with my heart. Lead my prayers, so that I say what you want me to say and quietly hear what you want me to hear. I believe that all things work together for good for those who love God. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.
prac: Admit you don’t know
Tell God in one sentence: “I don’t know how to pray about this.”
Invite the Holy Spirit
Say quietly, “Holy Spirit, please guide me in how to pray.”
Be still for one minute
Don’t rush to speak; notice any verse, picture or prompting that rises in your heart.
Test it by Scripture
Ask: Does this prompting agree with the Bible? Does it fit the character of Jesus? Does it bring love and peace?
Share humbly
When praying for others, share in the tone of “I sense this might be… what do you think?” rather than “God told me you will definitely…”
lessons.do: Today, use the five steps to pray about something you don’t know how to pray for. Write down in your prayer journal the prompting you received in the stillness, and note which verse you used to test it.
deep: Does praying in the Spirit always mean speaking in tongues?

Praying in tongues is a gift of the Holy Spirit, and the Bible affirms its value (1 Corinthians 14:2, 14:18); the Academy offers a separate course on it. But praying in the Spirit is broader: any prayer that submits to and is led by the Holy Spirit, whether with the understanding or with the spirit, is praying in the Spirit (1 Corinthians 14:15).
How do I know whether a prompting comes from the Holy Spirit?

The Spirit’s leading never contradicts Scripture; it exalts Jesus (John 16:14), bears the fruit of the Spirit such as love, joy and peace (Galatians 5:22-23), and can stand up to confirmation by spiritual companions. Be especially careful with promptings that bring control, fear, judgment or self-exaltation.
lessons.quick: When we don’t know how to pray as we ought, the Holy Spirit himself helps us pray.
text: In the same way, the Spirit also helps our weaknesses, for we don’t know how to pray as we ought. But the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can’t be uttered.
He who searches the hearts knows what is on the Spirit’s mind, because he makes intercession for the saints according to God.
We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.
lessons.keyText: In the same way, the Spirit also helps our weaknesses, for we don’t know how to pray as we ought. But the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can’t be uttered.

lessons.title: Intercession: Standing in the Gap
lessons.sub: Petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks for all
lessons.hear:
Paul wrote to young Timothy to teach him how to shepherd the church in Ephesus. Among all his instructions, he said: “I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men” (1 Timothy 2:1). “First of all” shows the priority of intercession in the life of the church: not a prayer tacked on after the activities, but intercession that comes before every ministry.

Paul uses four words. Petitions are urgent requests for specific needs. Prayers are our general speaking to God and worshiping him. Intercessions mean standing between another person and God and speaking on their behalf. Givings of thanks mean thanking God for people. Intercession is not just listing other people’s problems; it also includes thanking God for them. An intercessor who only “reports problems” easily grows heavier with every prayer; an intercessor who also gives thanks for people sees more and more of God’s work.

Paul also says to pray “for kings and all who are in high places, that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and reverence.” The scope of intercession is wide: from family to coworkers, from the church to the city, from those in authority to those who do not yet believe. Why? Because God “desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4). The motive of intercession is God’s heart of love for the world.

The Old Testament gives us a picture: God says he sought for someone to build up the wall and stand in the gap before him for the land (Ezekiel 22:30). An intercessor is someone who stands in the gap. Picture a flood breaking through a levee, and someone throwing themselves into the breach to hold back the water. Intercessors carry other people’s weakness, danger, and need in their prayers, standing before God and asking for mercy on their behalf. What an honorable ministry this is, and it is exactly what Jesus himself is doing now: he always lives to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25).

In the 321 life we practice 920 every day: each person in relationship with us is a “2,” we practice living out the selfless “0,” and we bear the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit, the “9.” Intercession is the most practical way to love our “2.” You may not be able to solve everyone’s problems, but you can bring their names before God every day. When we intercede for others, we turn from being centered on ourselves to being centered on others, from caring only about our own needs to carrying other people’s burdens.
lessons.light: Self-centered people pray only for themselves; selfless people stand in the gap for others. For Jesus, for others, not for ourselves: this is self-denying intercession. Intercession is one of the highest forms of love. Others may never know you are praying for them, but God knows, and his Kingdom spreads through this kind of hidden love.
think: What four kinds of prayer does Paul mention in 1 Timothy 2:1? How are they different?
Among my “2s” (family, coworkers, brothers and sisters), who have I not prayed for in a long time?
Is my intercession mostly “reporting problems,” or does it also include thanking God for people?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you that you always live to intercede for us. Make me someone who stands in the gap. Today I bring the people around me before you: my family, my coworkers, my brothers and sisters, and those who do not yet know you. Watch over them according to your will, and help me give thanks to you for them. I also pray for those in authority, that we may live in godliness and peace. May all people be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.
prac: List your “2s”
Write five names in your Prayer List: one each from your family, workplace, church, those who don’t yet believe, and those in authority.
One sentence of each kind
For each person, make one petition, pray one blessing, intercede for one need, and thank God for them once.
Asking beats guessing
When you have the chance, ask: “How can I pray for you?” Write down their answer.
Keep confidences
Never pass on prayer requests entrusted to you. Even in a prayer meeting, get permission before sharing.
Follow up
A few days later, check in: “I’ve been praying for you. How are things now?”
lessons.do: Today, create your “five-person prayer list” in the Prayer List and pray one sentence for each of them every day. This week, ask at least one of them: “How can I pray for you?”
deep: If I pray for many people, won’t it become routine?

It can, so it needs renewal. Use the Prayer List to take turns praying more deeply for different people, write down the latest requests as they come, and record answered prayers as testimonies. This keeps intercession full of fresh hope.
Should I pray even for politicians I don’t like?

When Paul wrote this letter, the ruler was the Roman emperor, who was not a Christian, yet Paul still told the church to pray for those in authority. Praying for leaders is not endorsing a position; it is asking God to rule, so that people may be saved and society may have peace.
lessons.quick: Intercession is standing in the gap and bringing other people’s names before God.
text: I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men,
for kings and all who are in high places, that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and reverence.
For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior,
who desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth.
lessons.keyText: I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men,

lessons.title: Listening and Asking
lessons.sub: What do you want me to do for you?
lessons.hear:
Blind Bartimaeus was sitting by the road outside Jericho. When he heard that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by, he cried out, “Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!” Many rebuked him and told him to be quiet, but he cried out all the more. And Jesus stood still. It is a moving scene: in a crowded, noisy throng, Jesus heard the cry of someone on the very margins.

Jesus had him brought over and then asked what seemed an unnecessary question: “What do you want me to do for you?” (Mark 10:51). Wasn’t it obvious what a blind man wanted? Yet Jesus did not assume; he asked. He gave this man back his dignity and let him voice his own need. Bartimaeus answered, “Rabboni, that I may see again.” Jesus said, “Go your way. Your faith has made you well.” Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus on the way.

This is the most important lesson in prayer ministry: listen first, then pray. When we pray for others, people have often said only two sentences before we rush to give answers, quote verses, and start praying. What we pray for is often the need we have guessed, not the person’s real need. It is like a doctor writing a prescription without examining the patient: even the best medicine can be given for the wrong problem.

Listening has three levels. First, hear what they say: what do they want me to pray for? Second, hear the heart they have not voiced: behind the problem, what are their real fears, wounds, and hopes? Third, hear the voice of the Holy Spirit: as they speak, what is the Spirit bringing to my attention? James says, “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Being swift to hear is where love begins.

Jesus’ question also shapes the attitude of our ministry. It is not “Here is what I am going to do for you,” but “What do you want me to do for you?” The main characters in ministry are not us, but God and the person in need. When we lay down our own judgments and are willing to listen and to ask, we are like Jesus standing still in the crowd, letting the overlooked person know: God has heard you.
lessons.light: Self-centered ministry rushes to speak because it wants to prove it is helpful; selfless ministry is willing to listen because its focus is on the other person and on God. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. A simple “What do you want me to do for you?” gives people back their dignity and hands the authority back to God.
think: In Mark 10:46-52, how was Jesus’ attitude toward Bartimaeus different from the crowd’s?
When I pray for others, do I tend to rush in with words, or am I willing to listen first?
Of the three levels of listening, which one do I most need to grow in?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for standing still in the noisy crowd and hearing the blind man’s cry, and for hearing my cry too. Give me a heart that is willing to listen, so that when I pray for others I will be quick to hear and slow to speak. Holy Spirit, help me hear the pain people have not put into words, and help me hear your voice. May I ask, as you did, “What do you want me to do for you?” In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.
prac: Stop
Put down your phone, turn toward the person, and tell them with your eyes and posture: I am listening.
Ask open questions
Ask: “How would you like me to pray for you?” “What worries you most about this?”
Reflect back
Say it back in your own words: “What I’m hearing is…. Is that right?”
Listen to the Spirit at the same time
While they speak, quietly ask in your heart: “Holy Spirit, what do you want me to pray for them?”
Short, focused prayer
Pray from what you have heard. It need not be long; let the person feel truly heard.
lessons.do: This week, before you pray for someone, listen for three minutes first: ask one open question, reflect back once to confirm, and only then pray. Afterward, ask them: “Did that prayer speak to your heart?”
deep: What if the person talks for a long time and I don’t know what to pray for?
You can gently ask: “If I could pray for just one thing, what would you most want God to do?” This helps them focus and makes your prayer more precise.
What if, while listening, I find their problem is serious and beyond my ability?

Pray for them first and show your care, then say honestly: “This is really important. I’d like to ask a more experienced coworker to walk with you too.” If there is self-harm, violence, or a serious physical or mental health condition, refer them to a pastor and professional help as soon as possible. Listeners do not have to carry everything alone.
lessons.quick: Ask “What do you want me to do for you?” before you begin to pray.
text: They came to Jericho. As he went out from Jericho with his disciples and a great multitude, the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting by the road.
When he heard that it was Jesus the Nazarene, he began to cry out and say, “Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!”
Many rebuked him, that he should be quiet, but he cried out much more, “You son of David, have mercy on me!”
Jesus stood still and said, “Call him.” They called the blind man, saying to him, “Cheer up! Get up. He is calling you!”
He, casting away his cloak, sprang up, and came to Jesus.
Jesus asked him, “What do you want me to do for you?” The blind man said to him, “Rabboni, that I may see again.”
Jesus said to him, “Go your way. Your faith has made you well.” Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus on the way.
lessons.keyText: Jesus asked him, “What do you want me to do for you?” The blind man said to him, “Rabboni, that I may see again.”

lessons.title: Praying in the Name of Jesus
lessons.sub: What I have, that I give you: authority comes from Jesus, not from me
lessons.hear:
“Peter and John were going up into the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour” (Acts 3:1). They were not going to a special conference; they were simply going to pray as usual. At the temple gate sat a man who had been lame from birth. He was carried there every day to beg. When he saw Peter and John, he asked them for money. It was an ordinary scene: two people on their way to pray met one person in need.

Peter, fastening his eyes on him, said, “Look at us.” The man paid attention, “expecting to receive something from them.” Then Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!” (Acts 3:6). He took him by the right hand and raised him up. Immediately his feet and ankle bones received strength, and he leapt up and went into the temple “walking, leaping, and praising God.”

“In the name of Jesus” is not a slogan to end our prayers; it is an identity and an authority. In ancient times, acting in the king’s name meant acting not on one’s own authority but by the king’s commission. Peter admitted, “I have no silver or gold”: he had no money, no status, no power of his own. But he had Jesus. What he gave was not his own; it was what he had received from Jesus. Jesus promised that whatever we ask in his name, he will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son (John 14:13).

Praying in Jesus’ name carries authority, and it also requires humility. There is authority because Jesus has already overcome everything, and his name is above every name. There is humility because this authority does not belong to us. When the crowd stared at Peter and John in amazement, Peter immediately asked them why they were staring, as if he and John had made this man walk by their own power or godliness (Acts 3:12). He turned the focus away from himself and back to Jesus.

This is the heart of the 321 path of service: let Jesus live in me and reign in me, and serve by his authority and power; everything is what God has done and accomplished in Jesus, so we give thanks in all things and give the glory to Jesus. Those who pray for others do not need to display their own spirituality. Like Peter, they only need to say, “What I have, that I give you,” and what we have is Jesus.
lessons.light: Self-centered servants want people to see their power; selfless servants let people see the name of Jesus. Praying in Jesus’ name means laying down our own name and lifting up his. The authority belongs to Jesus, the glory goes to Jesus, and I am simply a vessel that brings Jesus to people.
think: Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you.” What did he have?
In my prayers, is “in Jesus’ name” a habitual ending, or a declaration of faith?
When prayer is answered and people praise me, how can I turn the focus back to Jesus as Peter did?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, your name is above every name. I confess that I have no silver or gold, and no power of my own to change anyone. But I have you, and you live in me. Reign in me, and let me serve by your authority and power. When people are helped through prayer, may they see you and not me. Everything is your grace, and all the glory belongs to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.
prac: Look at the person
Like Peter, look at them so they know you truly care and are not just going through the motions.
Remember your identity
Before praying, remind yourself: I come in the name of Jesus, not on my own.
Brief and full of faith
Pray in Jesus’ name with clear words. There is no need to be loud or dramatic.
Respect and boundaries
Ask permission before laying on hands, place your hand only on the shoulder or head, and have a companion present when praying with someone of the opposite sex.
Give the glory to God
After praying, thank God together. Whatever the outcome, keep the focus on Jesus.
lessons.do: This week, when you pray for someone, deliberately begin by saying: “We come to the Father not in our own strength, but in the name of Jesus.” After praying, whatever the outcome, say a sentence of thanks to God together.
deep: Does praying in Jesus’ name guarantee that I will get what I ask for?

“In Jesus’ name” means praying according to Jesus’ heart and authority, not using his name as a guarantee. The purpose in John 14:13 is that the Father may be glorified in the Son. God hears whatever we ask according to his will (1 John 5:14); his answer is sometimes “yes,” sometimes “wait,” and sometimes a better “no.”
Do I need to pray loudly and forcefully to have authority?

Authority is not in volume; it is in Jesus. Peter’s prayer was very short and involved no special ritual. Quiet, faith-filled prayer in Jesus’ name carries the same authority. We should avoid drawing attention to our own performance.
lessons.quick: Authority comes from the name of Jesus, and the glory belongs to the name of Jesus.
text: Peter and John were going up into the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour.

A certain man who was lame from his mother’s womb was being carried, whom they laid daily at the door of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask gifts for the needy of those who entered into the temple.
Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive gifts for the needy.
Peter, fastening his eyes on him, with John, said, “Look at us.”
He listened to them, expecting to receive something from them.
But Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!”
He took him by the right hand and raised him up. Immediately his feet and his ankle bones received strength.
Leaping up, he stood and began to walk. He entered with them into the temple, walking, leaping, and praising God.
All the people saw him walking and praising God.
They recognized him, that it was he who used to sit begging for gifts for the needy at the Beautiful Gate of the temple. They were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.
lessons.keyText: But Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!”

lessons.title: Praying for the Sick and Suffering
lessons.sub: The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective
lessons.hear:
James speaks about prayer in a very down-to-earth way: “Is any among you suffering? Let him pray. Is any cheerful? Let him sing praises. Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the assembly, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord” (James 5:13-14). Suffering, joy, sickness: every situation in life can be brought before God.

This passage tells us that praying for the sick is a normal ministry of the church, and a shared one. The sick person “calls for the elders of the assembly” and does not face illness alone; the elders pray in the name of the Lord, showing that the whole family of God stands with them. In that day, anointing with oil had a medical meaning and also symbolized the Holy Spirit’s presence and being set apart for God. To pray for the sick is to place a person within God’s healing and the church’s love.

“The prayer of faith will heal him who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. If he has committed sins, he will be forgiven” (James 5:15). God is a God who heals, and we can pray for the sick with faith. But Scripture is also honest: Paul left Trophimus sick at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20), and Timothy was often ill, so Paul advised him to take a little wine (1 Timothy 5:23). Sometimes God heals immediately, sometimes he heals through medicine, and sometimes he gives grace that is sufficient in the midst of illness. So our faith is trust in God, not trust in a particular outcome.

Praying for the sick therefore takes faith, and it also takes love and wisdom. Never tell a sick person, “You weren’t healed because you don’t have enough faith”; that rubs salt into the wound. Never tell anyone to stop seeing a doctor or stop taking medication; medicine is also God’s grace. Our part is to be present, to listen, and to pray, placing the person’s body, emotions, family, and medical team into God’s hands.

James goes on: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective” (James 5:16). Healing is not only physical; it includes relationships and the soul. A “righteous person” is not a perfect person, but someone justified by faith and in right relationship with God and others. When we confess to one another and pray for one another in love, the church becomes a healing community.
lessons.light: When self-centered people pray for the sick, their focus is on the outcome, and they fear losing face if the prayer “doesn’t work.” When selfless people pray for the sick, their focus is on Jesus and the person, and they are willing to stay with them to the end. We cannot guarantee results, but we can guarantee presence. Praying for the sick is about helping them experience Jesus’ love in their suffering, not about proving our spirituality.
think: What situations does James 5:13-16 mention, and how should we respond to each?
Have I ever said something to a sick person that may have hurt them without my realizing it? What could I say from now on?
How could “confess your sins to one another and pray for one another” be practiced in my small group or with my spiritual companion?
lessons.speak: God who heals us, you are Jehovah Rapha, the LORD who heals. I bring before you those who are sick and suffering. Touch their bodies, comfort their hearts, and strengthen their families. Give wisdom to their doctors and medical teams. Lord, we believe you are able to heal, and we trust your good purposes; however you choose to work, let them experience your presence and peace. Help us confess to one another and pray for one another, and make us a healing community. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.
prac: Care first, then pray
Ask about their body, their feelings, and their family, then ask: “What would you most like God to do for you?”
Ask permission
Ask: “May I pray for you? May I put my hand on your shoulder?” Respect their choice.
Pray for the whole person
Pray for physical healing, peace of heart, strength for the family, and wisdom for the medical team.
No guarantees, no pressure
Don’t say “You will definitely get better,” and don’t say “Your faith isn’t strong enough.” Encourage them to keep receiving medical care.
Record and follow up
Note their needs in your ministry record and check in again in a few days. When needed, refer them to a pastor or elder.
lessons.do: This week, visit or contact someone who is sick or suffering. Pray for them using the five steps, create an entry in Praying for Others, and check in with them again three days later.
deep: If someone isn’t healed after I pray, is it my fault?

The sovereignty over healing belongs to God, not to the one praying. Our responsibility is to love and pray faithfully and leave the outcome to God. Even when Jesus was on earth, he did not heal every sick person (John 5:3-9). Staying humble and continuing to walk alongside them matters far more than finding out “whose fault” it is.
When should I refer someone for professional help?

When a person has thoughts of harming themselves or others, is experiencing violence, shows signs of serious depression or mental illness, or faces decisions about stopping medication or other medical choices, always encourage them to seek medical and professional help, and inform a pastor. Prayer and professional help do not conflict; both are gifts of grace that God uses.
lessons.quick: We cannot guarantee the outcome, but with faith and love we can place the sick into the hands of the Lord who heals.
text: Is any among you suffering? Let him pray. Is any cheerful? Let him sing praises.
Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the assembly, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord;
and the prayer of faith will heal him who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. If he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.
Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.
lessons.keyText: Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.

lessons.title: Praying in One Accord
lessons.sub: Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them
lessons.hear:
Peter and John were threatened by the Sanhedrin for preaching about Jesus and forbidden to speak in his name again. Once released, the first thing they did was return to their own company and tell everyone what had happened. When the believers heard it, “they lifted up their voice to God with one accord” (Acts 4:24). Faced with persecution, the early church’s first response was not to hold a meeting about strategy, but to pray together.

How did they pray? First, they addressed God as the one “who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them,” fixing their attention on his sovereignty. Next, they quoted Psalm 2 and saw that the persecution of their day was already under God’s control. Finally, their request was not “Remove our enemies” or “Keep us safe,” but: “Now, Lord, look at their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal; and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy Servant Jesus” (Acts 4:29-30).

The result: “When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness” (Acts 4:31). Prayer in one accord brings the presence and power of the Holy Spirit. Jesus also promised: “If two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them” (Matthew 18:19-20).

What is the key to being of one accord? Selflessness. Only the selfless can be one. If everyone comes to prayer carrying their own agenda, a prayer meeting becomes just another meeting, or even a contest of wills. Only when each person lays themselves down and fixes their eyes on Jesus can everyone share one heart and one mind. It is like an orchestra: the instruments are different, but they follow the same conductor. Not everyone plays the same notes, but everyone watches the same conductor.

In the 321 life we grow in 235 relationships: becoming “2” spiritual companions, building “3” spiritual parent-and-child relationships, and becoming “5” five-fold ministry teams. Prayer is the heart of all these relationships. When two spiritual companions pray together, when a small group prays together, when a team prays together, the power of the Holy Spirit flows among them and God’s Kingdom expands through them.
lessons.light: In a self-centered prayer meeting, everyone wants to persuade the others; in a selfless prayer meeting, everyone looks to Jesus. Only the selfless can be united, and only the selfless can overcome. Being of one accord does not mean having identical opinions; it means every heart is turned toward the same Lord. When together we give the Kingdom, the power, and the glory to God, the Holy Spirit moves among us.
think: In Acts 4:24-31, what parts make up the early church’s prayer? What did they ask for?
Are the prayer gatherings I attend more like “one accord” or “everyone saying their own thing”? Why?
Which spiritual companion could I begin praying with regularly?
lessons.speak: Lord, Creator of heaven and earth and everything in them, thank you for promising that where two or three gather in your name, you are there among us. Remove the self-centeredness from our hearts, so that we lay down our own agendas and look to you with one accord. When we face difficulties, we ask not only for peace, but for boldness to speak your word, and for you to stretch out your hand to heal. Fill us with your Holy Spirit and make us a team that prays in one heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.
prac: Find a prayer partner
Invite a spiritual companion to pray with you once a week at a set time. Even fifteen minutes is enough.
Worship first, then ask
Follow the order of Acts 4: first praise God’s sovereignty, then read a passage of Scripture, and only then make your requests.
Short prayers in turn
In a prayer meeting, each person prays only a sentence or two at a time, so more people can take part and no one prays at great length.
Follow the leader
The leader explains today’s prayer theme, and everyone prays around that one theme.
Say “Amen” together
When others pray, say “Amen” in your heart or aloud to show you are in agreement.
lessons.do: This week, invite a spiritual companion to pray with you for twenty minutes. You can use the Lead a Prayer Meeting tool to plan the flow: worship, Scripture, short prayers in turn, and blessing one another.
deep: What do we do when someone prays at great length in a prayer meeting?

The leader can gently explain at the start: “Today let’s each pray one or two sentences at a time, and we can go around several times.” This is not to restrict anyone, but to let more people take part and keep the prayer focused. You can also speak with the person privately in love.
Can people with different opinions pray together?

Yes, and they really need to. Being of one accord does not mean seeing everything the same way; it means submitting together before Jesus. In prayer we often find our positions softening, because our focus shifts from “who is right” to “what God wants.”
lessons.quick: Only the selfless can be one; prayer in one accord brings the presence and power of the Holy Spirit.
text: Being let go, they came to their own company and reported all that the chief priests and the elders had said to them.
When they heard it, they lifted up their voice to God with one accord and said, “O Lord, you are God, who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them;
who by the mouth of your servant David, said, ‘Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing?
The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers plot together, against the Lord, and against his Christ.’
“For truly, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed,
to do whatever your hand and your counsel foreordained to happen.
Now, Lord, look at their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness,
while you stretch out your hand to heal; and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy Servant Jesus.”
When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness.
lessons.keyText: Again, assuredly I tell you, that if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them.”

lessons.title: Watching and Multiplying
lessons.hear:
“When he finished praying in a certain place, one of his disciples said to him, ‘Lord, teach us to pray, just as John also taught his disciples’” (Luke 11:1). The disciples had followed Jesus, watched him do miracles, and heard him preach, yet what Scripture records them asking him to teach was prayer. A life of prayer is something that gets noticed, longed for, and passed on.

Jesus taught the disciples the Lord’s Prayer and then told a parable. A friend arrives at midnight, and you have no food in the house, so you knock on your neighbor’s door to borrow three loaves. The neighbor says the door is shut and the children are in bed. Jesus said, “Although he will not rise and give it to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence, he will get up and give him as many as he needs” (Luke 11:8). Then Jesus said, “Keep asking, and it will be given you. Keep seeking, and you will find. Keep knocking, and it will be opened to you” (Luke 11:9). The tense in the original language carries this sense of continuing to ask, seek, and knock. Prayer requires persistence.

Paul also says, “Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving” (Colossians 4:2). To continue steadfastly is not to give up easily; to watch is to stay alert like a watchman; to give thanks is to keep seeing God’s grace even while we wait. He also mentions a coworker, Epaphras, who was “always striving for you in his prayers” (Colossians 4:12). Epaphras wrote no letters and is rarely mentioned, but he was a watchman for the church. Every community of God’s people needs prayer watchmen like him.

Finally Jesus said, “If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke 11:13). The most precious answer to prayer is the Holy Spirit himself. When we pray persistently, God gives us not only what we ask for, but gives us himself.

One aim of 321 is to build God’s system. Prayer ministry cannot stop with one person; it must multiply. The last of the eight steps of changing mindsets is multiplication: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, and then multiplication. What you have learned in this course, teach to someone else; as you become a person of prayer, walk alongside another person as they become one too. As the life of prayer is passed on from generation to generation, God’s Kingdom expands on earth, and as we move toward the great end-time revival, we prepare to welcome the return of the Lord Jesus.
lessons.light: Self-centered people treat prayer as their own spiritual achievement; selfless people pass the life of prayer on to others. Multiplication is a mark of God’s system: I do not only pray myself, I also walk with others until they become people of prayer. Watching steadfastly, staying alert with thanksgiving, we see generation after generation of overcomers rise up in prayer.
think: In Luke 11:1-13, what different ways did Jesus use to teach his disciples to pray?
In my prayer life, what is the one thing that most needs “persistence”?
Which brother or sister could I walk with as they begin building a life of prayer? How will I start?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, teach us to pray, as you taught your disciples. Give me a heart that prays persistently, that stays alert with thanksgiving while I wait, and that does not give up easily. Thank you for giving the Holy Spirit to those who ask you; today I ask again: fill me with your Holy Spirit. Make me a watchman, and help me walk alongside many others as they become people of prayer. May the life of prayer be passed on from generation to generation, building God’s system and welcoming your return. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen.
prac: Choose what you will watch over
Choose one focus to watch over in prayer for the long term: a family, a small group, a church, or a city.
Keep a regular watch
Set a fixed time each week, such as Wednesday evening, to pray fifteen minutes for this focus.
Record and give thanks
Write down your prayers and God’s answers in your prayer journal, and review them regularly with thanksgiving.
Invite a companion
Invite someone younger than you, or someone just beginning to learn to pray, to pray with you.
Pass on one lesson
Use one lesson in this app to walk with them through see, hear, think, speak, and do.
lessons.do: Today, choose the focus you will watch over in prayer for the long term, and this week invite a companion to pray with you. When you finish this course, use Lesson 1 to help them start learning to pray, so the life of prayer keeps multiplying.
deep: How is persistent prayer different from “vain repetitions”?

“Vain repetitions” assume that God will listen if we say more words, so the focus is on technique. Persistent prayer refuses to give up because it trusts God, so the focus is on relationship. A child keeps asking their father not to persuade him, but because they believe in their father’s love.
My own prayer life isn’t good enough yet. Can I lead others in prayer?

Yes. Multiplication does not wait for perfection; we learn as we lead. If you are just one step ahead of someone, you can walk that step with them. Leading others in prayer is often the best way to renew your own prayer life.
lessons.quick: Keep watch persistently, and pass the life of prayer on to the next person.
text: When he finished praying in a certain place, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John also taught his disciples.”
He said to them, “When you pray, say, ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. May your Kingdom come. May your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven.
Give us day by day our daily bread.
Forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone who is indebted to us. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’”
He said to them, “Which of you, if you go to a friend at midnight and tell him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves of bread,
for a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him,’
and he from within will answer and say, ‘Don’t bother me. The door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I can’t get up and give it to you’?
I tell you, although he will not rise and give it to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence, he will get up and give him as many as he needs.
“I tell you, keep asking, and it will be given you. Keep seeking, and you will find. Keep knocking, and it will be opened to you.
For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened.
“Which of you fathers, if your son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, he won’t give him a snake instead of a fish, will he?
Or if he asks for an egg, he won’t give him a scorpion, will he?
If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?”
lessons.keyText: Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving,

verses.v: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
verses.p: Name each worry you carry today and hand them to God one by one, then thank him for one thing.

verses.v: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.
verses.p: Turn “he” into “you”: Lord, you are my shepherd; guide me in the paths of righteousness today.

verses.v: He gives power to the weak. He increases the strength of him who has no might. Even the youths faint and get weary, and the young men utterly fall; but those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.
verses.p: Pray for someone who is weary: ask the Lord to renew their strength, so they mount up with wings like eagles.

verses.v: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.
verses.p: Admit the limits of your own understanding, and hand one decision you are making to God for his direction.

verses.v: Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.
verses.p: Pray for someone who is afraid: God is with them and will uphold them with the right hand of his righteousness.

verses.v: that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love, may be strengthened to comprehend with all the saints what is the width and length and height and depth, and to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
verses.p: Following Paul’s prayer, ask God to strengthen this person in their inner being and help them know the love of Christ.

verses.v: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.
verses.p: Pray about one matter that needs wisdom, trusting God who gives to all liberally and without reproach.

verses.v: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
verses.p: Confess honestly, then declare: God is faithful and righteous, and he will forgive me.

verses.v: Praise the LORD, my soul! All that is within me, praise his holy name! Praise the LORD, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits, who forgives all your sins, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from destruction, who crowns you with loving kindness and tender mercies, who satisfies your desire with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.
verses.p: Pray for healing of body and soul, and count God’s blessings, not forgetting any of his benefits.

verses.v: Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.
verses.p: Find three things to be thankful for in your present situation, and name them one by one.

verses.v: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.
verses.p: Declare: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. Ask the Lord to reign over one specific thing today.

verses.v: But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.
verses.p: Place one need under God’s Kingdom and his righteousness, and seek his Kingdom first.

verses.v: If it seems evil to you to serve the LORD, choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.”
verses.p: Pray for your family members one by one, and declare: as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

verses.v: that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.
verses.p: Pray for unity in your church, small group, or team, so that the world may believe.

verses.v: Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore that the Lord of the harvest will send out laborers into his harvest.”
verses.p: Ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers, and ask yourself: for whom can I be a laborer?

verses.v: Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope in the power of the Holy Spirit.
verses.p: Pray for someone who is discouraged, asking the God of hope to fill them with all joy and peace.

lp.v: Pray like this: “‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
lp.p: Begin by worshiping God for who he is. Name one of his attributes, such as faithfulness, love, or holiness, and ask that his name be honored in your life.
lp.e: Father, you are the faithful God. May your name be kept holy in my home and on my lips.

lp.v: Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
lp.p: Ask Jesus to reign over one specific area: your heart, your family, your work, your church, your city.
lp.e: Lord Jesus, reign over my work, and let your Kingdom be seen there.

lp.v: Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
lp.p: Surrender one thing you want, saying: “Not my will, but yours, be done.”
lp.e: I have my own hopes about this, but I want your will to be done.

lp.v: Give us today our daily bread.
lp.p: Tell God your specific needs for today: daily life, work, health, relationships.
lp.e: Give me what I need for today, and provide for my family too.

lp.v: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
lp.p: Confess one specific sin, and forgive one person who has wronged you.
lp.e: Lord, forgive my impatience today. I also choose to forgive the person who hurt me.
